We were wrong. This week we learned of the URL savetheinlet.com. That address takes a viewer to a website titled “Restore Bushwick Inlet” that supports Gotham’s proposal, is full of imagery Gotham has used as part of its campaign, contains a link to Gotham’s petition, and links to Gotham’s Monitor Point website (at the URL monitorpointquay.com).

Acquiring similar domain names to mislead the public about a targeted website is a well-known dirty trick, with the use of .com addresses to mimic .org addresses being a classic example. While we of course have many concerns about the Gotham development proposal and understand you are working with a high-powered public-relations firm, we never for a moment thought Gotham would deploy such a deceitful tactic against an all-volunteer community group like ours.

Sincerely,

Katherine Thompson

c: Councilmember Lincoln Restler Community Board 1

March 30, 2026

Ms. Stephanie Shellooe, AICP Director, Environmental Assessment and Review Division New York City Department of City Planning (DCP)

New York, New York 10271

Re: Save the Inlet’s Public Comments for Monitor Point CEQR No. 25DCP068K / DEIS Dear Ms. Shellooe, Save the Inlet (STI) is opposed to the Monitor Point upzoning application by the Gotham Organization, the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) and the Greenpoint Monitor Museum (together, the Applicants). Save the Inlet views the Applicants’ draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) with alarm because it puts the project in a context that does not exist – where climate change is not accelerating and the adjacent land along the waterfront already zoned R8 for high density residential use will not continue to be built out to the existing zoning limits, straining the natural surroundings and infrastructure at every level. First, a threshold request. Save the Inlet members have attended the public meetings on Monitor Point and noticed that there are often large differences between what the Applicants say publicly and what is in their formal submission (for example, the public comments indicate even those most engaged largely believe the project is 40% affordable, but the application is for a 25% affordable project). We ask the DCP to require the Applicants to review their public presentations made throughout this process, redline the statements that were false at the time they were made, and to release those redlined documents to the public. Save the Inlet’s members have specific questions and concerns related to the Applicants’ DEIS. Appendix B: NYC Waterfront Revitalization Program: Consistency Assessment Form

“The Proposed Actions would facilitate a mixed-use development on the Development Site at 40 and 56 Quay Street” STI response: Please specify what alternative uses of the site were considered that (1) do not involve variances to the existing zoning; or (2) would allow more open space on the site, or (3) would allow the MTA Lot 1 to become a park. If the answer to any of these options is none, please explain the rationale for not considering such an alternative. Monitor Point “would be comprised of three buildings totaling approximately 1,214,000 gross square foot [sic] . . . including residential space for up to 1,150 total dwelling units” STI response: Please explain the rationale for placing 1,150 families in a NYC Evacuation Zone 1, in buildings planned to be up to 600 feet tall. Please provide the evacuation plan for those families. Please also explain which floors of each building in the proposed development, if any, are considered “subject to flooding” under New York City’s Building Codes, and what restrictions on their use are planned. Monitor Point will have “approximately 37,000 gsf of below-grade parking (approximately 140 spaces) on Lot 1. STI response: Please explain the rationale for placing underground parking on a Zone 1 floodplain, and the flood evacuation plan for that space. Monitor Point will “include the creation of over an acre of waterfront open space (approximately 50,000 sf or 1.15 acres). STI response: Please detail what portion of that space will be accessible to the public, and what portion will not be, and specify the particular uses of each space, indicating square footage and acreage. Please also specify what amount of the open space will be porous ground, and for the portions that are impermeable, identify their uses and level of impermeability. The proposal includes payments of “$300,000 annually . . to the City/NYC Parks for the operation of Bushwick Inlet Park” STI response: Please specify if NYC Parks has agreed to make any changes to the existing Bushwick Inlet Park to accommodate the proposed Monitor Point project, and the cost of any such changes. Please identify in detail any portion of Bushwick Inlet Park that would be ripped up if the Monitor Point project is developed, the amount of time the land will be inaccessible to the public, and the rationale for allowing these actions. Please specify the net present value of any contributions the developer will make to NYC Parks, and of any costs to NYC Parks incurred by the proposed development.

The Proposed Development would also include resiliency and flood protection measures on the Development Site including installation of a new bulkhead to defend against future flooding due to sea level rise, implementation of wet floodproofing for non-critical and dry floodproofing for critical features.” STI response: Please explain what work has been done to assess the impact of this proposed development on the resiliency and flood protection for the surrounding community. Please include within that not only possible future floods, but storm surges and changes in the water table. Please indicate the size of the surrounding community included in any such assessments – both the distance from the site covered and the number of people living within the area. Please provide information on how any water blocked from Monitor Point’s luxury tower by the bulkhead and podium is expected to flow. We are concerned that the bulkhead could amplify wave action, increase erosion along the adjacent shoreline, and sever the natural relationship between the upland and the tidal inlet. If you disagree with these ideas, please explain why. Provide any assessment concerning the impact of this upzoning on water events within the half mile study zone, including Bushwick Inlet, the existing buildings and planned buildings that can be built as of right, the MTA tunnels through Greenpoint and Williamsburg, and the Greenpoint Avenue and Nassau Street subway stations. Given that Lot 1 is owned by the MTA, we expect that the environmental assessment would include any impact on the MTA’s existing infrastructure including the nearest two train stations. If that is not so, please state so clearly. Provide information on how this development will impact the combined sewer system assuming the neighboring area is developed to the full amount allowable under current zoning. Provide information on how this development will impact the combined sewer system assuming the neighboring area is developed to the full amount allowable under current zoning. If the answer to any of these questions is that such work has not been done, please explain the rationale. (We have more detailed concerns on this issue in the water section below.) The Applicants claim “The current proposal is the fulfillment of the City’s vision for this site as established by the 2005 rezoning”. STI response: This statement is clearly false, as the Applicants seek a massive upzoning from the 2005 rezoning in place. Please provide an explanation of whether the Applicants

considered using the site consistent with the current R6 zoning, and whether they considered a development without an upzoning feasible, and if not, why not. The Waterfront Revitalization Plan expects to support and facilitate commercial and residential redevelopment in areas well-suited to such development, and to encourage commercial and residential redevelopment in appropriate Coastal Zone areas. STI response: The Applicants have not adequately addressed the “well-suited” and “appropriate coastal zone” portion of the siting requirements. While the Applicants acknowledge the land they hope to build on is both adjacent to and partially within Community Board 1’s only “recognized ecological complex” that should be protected, placing luxury towers on the land is not a solution that makes any sense. The Applicants plan to fortify this parcel without adequately internalizing the cost to the people and natural resources around it. The Applicants claim the proposed development enhances public access to the waterfront compared to the existing building. STI response: The existing NYCTA facility has existed for decades as a single-story industrial building much like the surrounding buildings along Franklin and upland Greenpoint. It is not out of character. However, the proposed enormous trio of high rises will dramatically change the character of Quay Street from historic industrial Greenpoint waterfront with light and air into a massive wall pushed up against the sidewalk soaring 21 stories, a multi-story podium with 2 high rise towers protruding at 41 and 56 stories. This will obliterate light from the South casting Quay Street and upland Greenpoint into shadow. Contrary to DEIS, the views will be obliterated. The connector street, which the Applicants claim credit for, is required by the zoning restriction. The Applicants say: “a key element of the Proposed Development design is the protection and restoration of natural resources within and adjacent to Bushwick Inlet, including its habitats, flora, and fauna. Accordingly, the Applicant is undertaking extensive shoreline restoration as part of the proposed waterfront open space, including shoreline stabilization to address existing erosion and sedimentation impacts to Bushwick Inlet, as well as habitat restoration and establishment. In contrast to the current dominance and proliferation of nonnative/invasive plant species at the Development Site under existing conditions, the planting plan for the Proposed Development includes the installation of native tree, shrub, and herbaceous plant species that occur in New York coastal habitats.” STI response: The Applicants’ description of their project is self-serving and disingenuous, to say the least, as the main feature of the project is a 40-foot steel bulkhead that hardens the shoreline, while the two largest towers will be built over an enormous podium encompassing a great deal of the parcel’s land. STI requests that the proposed plan be compared to a natural

alternative that would protect and restore the tidal wetlands and allow the shoreline and land to provide a buffer to the surrounding neighborhood and adjacent embayment. We are concerned that the applicant’s response to the policy guidelines to protect natural resources are not detailed enough in how the proposed project will impact the area. • We ask how placing three high rise towers on 1.8 acres of land 50 feet from the water's edge of the Bushwick Inlet will impact the environment in a positive way and protect vulnerable plant, fish and wildlife species, and rare ecological communities?

• How would an excavation to support these enormous towers impact the already full water table on the land? Will construction disturb toxic soil and compounds, and shift contaminated soil and water to the Bushwick Inlet? A portion of Bushwick Inlet Park has been built out and now contains new rip rap, marsh edge, and earthen berm. How will this be protected?

• The proposal claims to enhance wetlands and vegetated tidal high and low marsh plant communities. However, the plan is an elevated walkway that can be described as a narrow esplanade, and contains a variance request to reduce the waterfront access plan area from 40 feet to 30 ft. How can the plan be reconciled with the claims? The Waterfront Revitalization Plan looks to protect the quality and quantity of groundwater, streams, and the sources of water for wetlands. The Bushwick Inlet is the outlet for the historic Bushwick Creek which began in Bushwick and meandered through the marshy wetlands until it reached the East River and Bushwick Inlet tidal estuary. This creek still runs underground along N.15th Street and it is visible in daylight puddling and floods during weather events. 40 Quay sits on landfilled wetlands and the historic Creek is still active today. (Please see Exhibit E). How can the Applicants reconcile the plan to place an enormous podium that spans over 60% of the Monitor Point footprint, creating a hardened landscape abutting the narrow 50' wide Bushwick Inlet Park with this obligation to protect the groundwater? Save the Inlet contends the abundant hardscape in the design is counter to goals of the Waterfront Revitalization Plan which emphasizes nature-based designs. The Waterfront Revitalization Plan looks to integrate consideration of the latest New York City projections of climate change and sea level rise (as published in New York City Panel on Climate Change 2015 Report, Chapter 2: Sea Level Rise and Coastal Storms) into the planning and design of projects in the city’s Coastal Zone.

STI notes that building Monitor Point in a flood zone goes against New York State’s and City’s own recommended policies. New York State issued revised FEMA assessment in 2025 (found here: NYSClimateimpacts.org). The new assessment predicts the sea-level in the Bushwick Inlet will be 23" higher by 2050, less than 20 years from the proposed build date of this project. The assessment strongly recommends that publicly owned properties on climate risk waterfront should not be developed into residential housing. How can this project on government agency land be reconciled with that directive? The Waterfront Revitalization Plan seeks to minimize environmental degradation and negative impacts on public health from solid waste, toxic pollutants, hazardous materials, and industrial materials that may pose risks to the environment and public health and safety. This project would require a Brownfield remediation. What is the projected range of cost of such a remediation, and how much of that cost would be covered by the taxpayers either (1) directly or (2) indirectly through tax incentives, rebates, or other means? How much, for how long, and by what methods are toxic materials expected to be transported from the site in the remediation process? The Waterfront Revitalization Plan seeks to Provide public access to, from, and along New York City's coastal waters. Save the Inlet contends that the proposed development would not enliven the waterfront, instead it would ruin the public Bushwick Inlet Park by building enormous, bulky buildings adjacent to the park and only 50' from the water's edge, essentially privatizing the public park as an amenity for the high-rise dwellers. We refer the Department to the Alternative vision Nick Shannon has proposed, which is attached to this submission. Water and Sewar Infrastructure For context, according to NYC Overview of Climate, the sea level around New York City is rising twice as fast as the global average. When the ground is easily saturated, more stormwater will run off into streets and homes. The City’s average annual rainfall is increasing at a rate of almost an inch per year, according to the Department of Environmental Protection. The Bushwick Inlet is in a designated flood zone within Evacuation Zone 1 at the site of historic wetland marshes. The water table in Greenpoint is full. As recently as July 2025, an everyday downpour dropped 2.7 inches of rain on the city in just an hour. In 2021, Hurricane Ida left nine inches of rain, falling at a peak rate of 3.47 inches per hour in Central Park, record breaking for the City. New York City’s sewar capacity is just 1.75 inches per hour. During Hurricane Sandy 14 years ago, storm surge rose 12ft at the Bushwick Inlet. Greenpoint sewers were completely overwhelmed and homes were flooded.

The CEQR manual lists the thresholds where a project’s potential to result in a significant adverse impact to the environment. A preliminary infrastructure analysis would be needed if the project is located in a combined sewer area and would exceed the following incremental development of residential units or commercial, public facility, and institution and/or community facility space above the predicted No-Action scenario: (1) 1,000 residential units or 250,000 sq. ft. of commercial, public facility, and institution and/or community facility space or more in Manhattan; or, (2) 400 residential units or 150,000 sq. ft. of commercial, public facility, and institution and/or community facility space or more in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Staten Island, or Queens. This project meets these thresholds, so STI offers these questions to the Dept of City Planning commissioners to consider: • Has the proposed development adequately plan for its massive overloading of a sewer overflow system already at overcapacity? • Has the proposal adequately explained the feasibility of connecting the MP development to existing sewer infrastructure? • Has the proposal contributed to or harmed climate change preparedness and investment in long term infrastructure solutions for Greenpoint? • Given that the project exceeds 400 residential units and is located within the Newtown Creek combined sewer drainage area, can DCP clarify whether a full detailed hydraulic analysis (not just preliminary analysis) was conducted, as recommended in the CEQR Technical Manual for areas of concern? • Have the Applicants studied how the extra wastewater generated by their development could potentially adversely affect marine life in these bodies of water and park goers who inhale air during these periods of released wastewater? • The CEQR Technical Manual identifies Newtown Creek as a sensitive drainage area requiring infrastructure assessment. How does the DEIS account for this designation beyond standard threshold analysis? • Has the study area appropriately included all downstream infrastructure components, including regulators, interceptors, and CSO outfalls such as NCB-004 and NCB-005? The proposal also raises concerns around Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO) Impacts. During rain events, the NCB-004 CSO’s are discharged in the Bushwick Inlet. The average discharge is 164 million gallons per year for the Bayside (Southside of mouth of the Bushwick inlet park site) and 19 million gallons per year for the Quay Street / Monitor Park site BEFORE the addition of the thousands of the proposed project’s toilets and showers.

• The DEIS concludes that the project would not result in a significant adverse impact because flows represent a small percentage of WRRF capacity. How does this conclusion account for localized CSO conditions, where impacts are driven by peak flow and storm events, not plant capacity alone? (For context, Greenpoint- Bushwick Creek Watershed is within the 12 ft flood zone, which was reached during Hurricane Sandy). • Existing data indicates significant annual CSO discharge volumes at Bushwick Inlet and along Quay Street. How does the DEIS evaluate the project’s contribution to cumulative CSO volumes and frequency, particularly during wet weather events? • Was CSO modeling conducted, as recommended in the CEQR Technical Manual when increases may exacerbate overflow events such as the recent extreme weather events? If not, why not? • Did the DEIS model cloudburst and other storm surge flooding impacts upon upland areas? If not, why not? • How does the project align with the City’s Long-Term Control Plan (LTCP) commitments for Newtown Creek, which are intended to reduce—not increase—CSO discharges? We ask the DCP to require detailed analysis under Peak Flow and Real-World Usage Scenarios. (We also refer you to Exhibits A – D showing the local sewer maps including the CSOs). This proposed development is not happening in isolation, it would compound population density with new residential construction. • The analysis references average daily flow increases. How does the DEIS account for peak discharge scenarios, such as simultaneous residential usage (e.g., large-event usage spikes), which can stress combined sewer systems? • What assumptions were used for per capita wastewater generation, and how do these translate to total flows for approximately 1,100+ residential units? Did the study include anticipated new population density? • Can DCP provide the maximum instantaneous flow estimates, rather than only daily averages? • How does the analysis take into account expected as of right development nearby? According to CB1 there are 4600 new as-of-right housing units being planned for West Street from Quay to Greenpoint Ave. From what we can see, these are not included in the modeling for impacts on sewer capacity demands. In addition, properties on

Greenpoint Ave are being prepared to be sold or re-developed. CB1 estimates 15,000 new residents within a two-block radius of Monitor Point. Save the Inlet is concerned with the project’s burden on sewer capacity and infrastructure constraints. • The project discharges to a 36-inch combined sewer leading to a 66-inch pipe and downstream interceptors. What is the existing utilization rate and available capacity of these pipes during dry and wet weather conditions? • Has a hydraulic capacity analysis been performed for the Franklin Street interceptor system, including the 96” x 90” interceptor, to confirm it can accommodate additional flows? • Will any off-site sewer upgrades or enlargements be required to accommodate the project? If so, where are these disclosed? • How will the addition of 15,000 new residents impact the demands on the capacity of the Franklin St interceptor system • Recently, the city announced the redesign of the long-term control plan at Newtown Creek —a small waterway that separates Brooklyn and Queens and connects to the East River—causing delays in the reduction of combined sewer overflow into the creek. Though the redesign would lead to a 67 percent reduction in overflow into the creek, rather than 62 percent, community leaders want to see further reductions if the project is to be delayed to 2040. How would this project further strain that system? STI concerns regarding Elevation, Pumping, and Flood Risk (see Chapter 11, p. 9 figure 11-1) Does the DEIS model scenarios for 2040 (less than 25 years) when NYS predictions of sea-level rise is 23”? • How will the sewer pipes from the west end of Quay connect to Franklin given the grade? • Flow Requirements: The invert elevation of the outfall must be lower than the upstream pipe to ensure gravity-driven flow. What is the invert elevation and depth of the receiving sewer infrastructure, and how does this affect system reliability under flood conditions? • Given that portions of the site appear to be at a lower elevation than downstream connections (e.g., Franklin Street), will the project require pumping systems to convey wastewater?

• If pumping of water is required: o What are the design flood elevations for pump equipment? o What redundancy and backup power systems are proposed? o How does the DEIS assess failure risk during flood events, when pumps are most vulnerable? STI concerns regarding Stormwater Management and Best Management Practices (BMP) effectiveness The DEIS relies on Best Management Practices (BMPs) such as detention tanks and green infrastructure. Can DCP please provide: • The required retention volume for the site? • The assumed performance during extreme storm events, not just small rainfall events? • Reduce density and wastewater generation? • Increase on-site retention beyond minimum requirements? • How will BMP performance be ensured over time, and what enforcement mechanisms are in place? • Given climate projections, were BMP systems evaluated under future rainfall intensity scenarios? • Where will the tanks be placed, and how will they be protected from climate events? STI concerns regarding Floodplain and System Interaction • The project is located within a designated floodplain area. How does the DEIS evaluate the interaction between: o Storm surge flooding, and o Combined sewer system backflow or surcharge conditions? • Could flooding conditions lead to untreated sewage discharge into the East River via outfalls such as NCB-004? STI concerns regarding Regulatory Consistency and Compliance- Cumulative and Future Conditions

• How does the conclusion of “no significant adverse impact” align with (1) Clean Water Act requirements, and (2) Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) permit obligations, which require reductions in pollutant discharge? • Has the project been evaluated for consistency with citywide stormwater management goals, including reducing CSO events and improving water quality? • How does the DEIS account for cumulative development in the North Brooklyn waterfront and its impact on the combined sewer system? • Were future climate conditions, including increased rainfall intensity and sea level rise, incorporated into the infrastructure analysis? STI concerns regarding Alternatives and Resilience Planning- Bushwick Creek Watershed Catchment Zone Bushwick Inlet sits within historic wetlands which reach all the way from the East River past McCarren Park. • Given the location within the Bushwick Inlet watershed, was the site evaluated as part of a broader flood mitigation or stormwater capture strategy, similar to NYC’s Cloudburst initiatives? Given the project’s location within a combined sewer system, a designated drainage area of concern, and a flood-prone waterfront, Save the Inlet’s position is that a more robust, sitespecific, and future-oriented analysis is warranted to fully assess potential impacts on wastewater and stormwater infrastructure. Open Space Save the Inlet is concerned the proposed development will directly and severely degrade the design and user experience of Bushwick Inlet Park. We ask the DCP to consider the quality of the open space available to the public. Erecting 640’, 490’, and 260’ towers abutting the inlet section of the park will negate the ‘open’ aspect of open space here. A development of this scale towering so close to the inlet and the park will be oppressive in its visual impact. It will effectively serve as the front yard for about 3,000 people, who are primarily in the top 10% of income earners, who will live in these immense towers, which will have the net effect of privatizing the park. Public parks are the great equalizer, and should be open and inviting to all, regardless of background and economic status. The out-of-scale with-action development will lessen the park’s essential feeling of openness and as being an inviting, welcoming space within the public realm.

STI is also concerned with the amount of open space available to the public in the Greenpoint and Williamsburg neighborhoods. For decades, Brooklyn Community District #1 has ranked in the bottom percentile for Open Space Ratio (OSR) in the City, at a measly .6 acres per 1,000 people, where the City average is 1.8 acres and the City’s goal is 2.5 acres. The proposed development will lower the local ratio even further with the addition of nearly 3,000 new residents, because the small amount of open space in this project does not even keep pace with the existing low open space ratio, because it would add so many residents. STI urges the Department of City Planning to expand the scope of its open space review to capture the reality of a fast-growing residential neighborhood. Consideration must be given to the tsunami of new waterfront and upland development in Greenpoint and North Williamsburg over the last 20 years, which has shown no signs of slowing down. Tens of thousands of new residents have moved into these areas, especially on the East River waterfront near the 40 Quay site. Current nearby public open spaces are inundated to full capacity during peak periods. Natural Resources The Bushwick Inlet is a unique tidal embayment and estuary, the only registered ecological complex within the Community District. It is a remnant of the original marshland and the Bushwick Creek, which fed and protected the shoreline. This vital ecosystem supports both breeding and migrating marine life and an enormous array of avian species that breed, winter, and migrate through the environs of the Inlet. The building height and number of windows in the proposed project could be devastating to thousands of migrating birds, as they could fall victim to window collisions, despite the 2019 City legislation that protects new construction up to 70 feet. This phenomenon is currently happening at epic levels in the New York City area, as this region lies along a major avian migratory flyway (the Atlantic Flyway). Our geographic location as a City poses an immense challenge for the billions of birds that migrate twice a year along the Atlantic flyway. The documentation provided in the DEIS is not comprehensive in capturing the vulnerabilities posed by human interaction (e.g., habitat loss, lead poisoning, various types of pollution). “Artificial light at night (ALAN) is a rapidly expanding pollutant, raising concerns about its impact on species that rely on natural light cues for critical behaviors” (Winter, 2025). Applicants state (in Appendix E, page 2) The avian species listed below were observed (i.e., seen and/or heard) during field surveys conducted on January 8 and April 18, 2025 (*indicates species observed within Bushwick Inlet and/or Bushwick Inlet Park). This observed bird species list is not intended to be an all-inclusive inventory of the avian species present at the Development Site.

Indeed, the list fails to capture the avian species seen in the area, especially given the continuous nature of the waterfront shoreline conveyed in the Waterfront Plan, and the adjacent areas utilized for nesting, foraging, and rest (e.g., Bushwick Inlet Park’s parcels at 86 or 50 Kent, WNY Transmitter Park, or even the immediate West Wharf’s park). The provided list also fails to take into account the Near Threatened species, Killdeer (Charadrius vociferus), which have actively used the span of the waterfront as their nesting grounds “Killdeer are often found away from shores as well as near them, frequenting mudflats, gravel bars, short-grass meadows, and their twentieth-century counterparts, such as construction sites, road shoulders, gravel roads and driveways, graveled rooftops, lawns, pastures, and golf courses” with nesting beginning in “May in the northern tier of states and southern Canada.” Already seen in March 2026, this returning nesting migrator was also seen on the Inlet’s soft shore beach via a local Naturalist, July 6, 2025, where adults and juveniles were observed (https://ebird.org/species/killde/L2987635) directly in front of the 40 Quay site. This specific species of birds is active both day and night, creating immense challenges for concurrent construction projects in North Brooklyn and Long Island City, where citizen scientists have documented their sightings on Cornell’s eBird platform (Jackson, B. J., & Jackson, J. A., 2020). Continued research needs for these taxa of bird are needed, specifically, “Nocturnal behavior of the species has received scant attention. In particular, more information is needed on the extent of feeding at feeding, possible variation in nocturnal foraging with moon phase, the roles of the sexes in incubation and brooding at night, and the nature of social interactions at night”—while research may not be conducted at this site, the proposition of a highlighted need for the data suggests a vulnerability to the species based on the prioritized behaviors as noted by Jackson and Jackson (2020). Additionally, this population of birds has been identified as particularly sensitive to collisions with stationary and moving objects, such as buildings—the MTA’s single-story height poses minimal conflict with their migratory passage. Noted as “more” prone than other shorebirds to strike television towers and tall buildings during nocturnal movements. Because the gravel aprons frequently present along roadsides are attractive to this species as potential nest sites, and the raised open beds of roads are attractive as display sites, Killdeer are particularly vulnerable to being struck by vehicles” (Jackson, B. J., & Jackson, J. A., 2020). Further, while we have over 150 species recorded at Bushwick Inlet Park, it doesn’t account for all 408 migratory bird species that utilize the Atlantic flyway, or the 280 birds known to pass through New York City during migration. Additionally, the Natural Resources section does not investigate the IUNC Red List categories of species (23, 6% globally threatened) that have been noted in the inlet and the subsequent protections to ensure their continued
rebound, given the 2025 State of Birds (in appendices) deep concern about the accelerated decline and impact on humans and our environment (NABCI, 2025).

Figure 1- IUCN Red List Category of Species, American Flyways, The IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria are an objective and widely accepted system for classifying species according to their extinction risk. Species are divided into eight categories—Extinct (EX), Extinct in the Wild (EW), Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN), Vulnerable (VU), Near Threatened (NT), Least Concern (LC), and Data Deficient (DD). Those categorized as Vulnerable, Endangered, or Critically Endangered are considered globally threatened Species on the IUNC Red List observed in the Inlet include: • Chimney Swift (Chaetura pelagica) • Horned Grebe (Podiceps auritus) • Greater Yellowlegs (Tringa melanoleuca) • Killdeer (Charadrius vociferus) • Blackpoll Warbler (Setophaga striata) What protections are in place for this animal life, which face multiple threats from this project? The New York City Bird Alliance’s DBird.org is a citizen-science portal for documenting avian deaths from reported collisions in North America. The Wild Bird Fund (the only wildlife rehabilitation center in the five boroughs) continues to see window-collision injuries and deaths despite the City’s new construction requirements for new buildings—these compulsory additions nevertheless did not account for additional factors involved with collisions such as light pollution, whether from construction or residents, which can create fatigue, and disorientation leading to collisions with a structure. The State of the Birds report: United States of America. North American Bird Conservation Initiative. https://www.stateofthebirds.org/2025/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/state-of-the-birds-sotb- 2025-pages.pdf is a useful source of information on birds.

While the design of the building is not a wall of glass, collisions still are possible above the 70-foot mark of protection, as well as the physical disruption of the airspace so close to the water’s edge. Additionally, habitat loss, construction impacts, various types of pollution, and the threat of car strikes are not eliminated by the 70 feet of bird-friendly building materials required by City law. ALAN not only increases the likelihood of collisions but can also influence marine life (Winter, 2025). Less than 150 feet from the water, this proposed project would inherently impact estuary wildlife and the East River ecosystem, including other forms of life beyond reptiles and mammals. Naturalists have recently observed Diamondback Terrapins (Malaclemys terrapin), an endangered species, nesting on land slated for development and in areas of Bushwick Inlet Park that would be disrupted by the proposed project. According to the National Fish and Wildlife Service (2025), “homes closer to the shoreline or with bright lights near windows may need [a] darker tint […] to effectively eliminate light” that disorients and disrupts the quality of life for the protected species noted, as well as the other wildlife in the proposed project corridor. At the time of authorship, New York State and the City of New York had no lighting requirements or standards enacted to minimize light pollution after 9 PM during the migratory or nesting seasons, both critical times for their continued distribution. Relying upon developer or builderdriven intervention has shown promise; however, researchers recommend additional measures of protection given the “unrealistic and unlikely to enact meaningful change given the sweeping geographic need, not just in North America but worldwide “to help navigate the complexity and confusion associated with enforcing national and regional (provincial and state) legislation around ALAN, and building materials (Klem, 2025). Killdeer and Diamondback Terrapins face threats as species from human conflict, including habitat loss, pollution (including light pollution, which disorients both marine and terrestrial species), and car strikes. Additionally, how will pile driving and drilling potentially adversely affect marine life in the inlet? Transportation [T]he Proposed Development would generate 206 subway passengers in the northbound direction through the Greenpoint Avenue station maximum load point during the weekday AM peak hour. The increase in subway passengers per car would be 4.58. The Proposed Development would generate 97 subway passengers in the southbound direction through the 21st Street station maximum load point during the weekday AM peak hour. The increase in subway passengers per car would be 3.95. As these passenger-per-car increments are both less than five passengers per car, significant adverse impacts to subway line haul conditions are not anticipated.

The impact on subway crowding is quite close to what seems to be an arbitrary limit on when an increase in ridership will be perceptible. As the study shows, the G line in Greenpoint is operating at and over capacity during peak hours. Adding four passengers per car to an overcapacity car is more impactful than adding four passengers to a car where there’s space. Particularly given that the proposed project site is MTA owned, why does the proposal not attempt to mitigate the proposed project’s anticipated contribution to overcrowding? STI also encourages the DCP to consider the impact of the project in instances of climate events. Wind Wind Impacts on Migratory Birds & Public Open Space Save the Inlet doesn’t think that the Pedestrian-Level Wind (PLW) Study included in Appendix D of the Monitor Point DEIS sufficiently evaluates wind impacts on both migratory birds and passive recreation conditions at Bushwick Inlet Park, a recognized ecological complex and critical public open space resource. The report concludes that wind conditions are “acceptable” because they do not exceed a 56 mph gust threshold. According to The National Weather Service, official Beaufort Wind Scale, 39-46 mph are “Gale” force winds. Winds at 56 mph are registered as level “Storm- trees uprooted; considerable structural damage occurs.” This seems like an inappropriately high bar that ignores widely accepted thresholds for comfort, usability, and everyday safety in an urban environment. In New York City, winds in the range of 40 to 50 mph are already considered dangerous, creating walking difficulties, increasing the risk of falling debris, and making streets and open spaces hazardous. The National Weather Service issues High Wind Warnings when sustained winds reach 40 mph, and pedestrian balance is known to be significantly affected at gusts around 55 mph. It is notable that the DEIS Wind Study itself predicts conditions approaching approximately 39 mph, with multiple locations reaching into the mid-40 mph range. These are not trivial conditions—they are borderline dangerous for pedestrians and widely recognized as uncomfortable and unsuitable for passive recreation. This is especially concerning given the site’s immediate adjacency to Bushwick Inlet Park, which is intended to serve as a place for sitting, relaxing, waterfront viewing, children’s play, and informal gathering. CEQR requires evaluation of whether a project would diminish the usability of public open space. Winds in the 30 to 45 mph range on are well known to discourage sitting and lingering, create harsh and unpleasant conditions along waterfronts, and will reduce the overall accessibility and enjoyment of Bushwick Inlet Park. Save the Inlet believes that the DEIS does not meaningfully evaluate these comfort and usability thresholds and deserves more scrutiny.

The Wind Study does not include consideration of impacts on migratory and habitating birds in the inlet. Save the Inlet thinks this is a severe oversight and study of wind impacts on birds and ecology should be studied. Winds in the range of 25 to 30 mph are known to begin stressing birds and disrupting migration, while gusts of 35 to 40 mph or higher can force landings, displace birds from flight paths, and impair navigation (NYC Bird Alliance). The project, however, is predicted to generate wind conditions at approximately 39 mph sustained equivalents, with gusts in the mid-40 mph range—levels that exceed thresholds known to disrupt bird behavior. The Bushwick Inlet is a recognized migratory corridor in Eastern Long Island and a designated ecological complex identified in the Waterfront Revitalization Program. Bushwick Inlet functions as a critical stopover and navigation point, where birds depend on relatively calm conditions to land, rest, and feed. The DEIS Wind Study should study the impact from the bird’s point of view where the construction of three high-rise towers—21, 41, and 56 stories—directly adjacent to this habitat which could generate downwash, wind acceleration, and turbulent shear zones that can increase energy expenditure, cause disorientation, and lead to migration “fallout” events where birds are forced to land in suboptimal and hazardous urban environments. These impacts should be analyzed in the DEIS. The wind study does not thoroughly look at cumulative neighborhood conditions because it does not include anticipated as-of-right development along West Street extending north toward Greenpoint Avenue. The combined impact of the proposed Monitor Point towers, existing high-rise development, and likely future buildout could result in a continuous corridor of elevated wind conditions along West Street and into Bushwick Inlet Park. Without modeling this reasonably foreseeable full build-out scenario, Save the Inlet does not believe that the DEIS Wind Study meets CEQR requirements and should be expanded to include all of West St. Save the Inlet questions why the Wind Study only models conditions at approximately five feet above grade, which is irrelevant to bird flight behavior. The model explicitly excludes vegetation and landscape features which seems peculiar as we know is affected by wind. The study also excludes extreme weather events such as Hurricanes and Super Storms, despite increasing climate volatility, and does not integrate its findings with ecological or open space impact analyses. Last July 2025, NYC experienced several very damaging “storms” which brought gusty winds of 50-65 mph to the NYC area, resulting in downed trees and power line damage, and massive flooding. It seems at the very least, the wind study should include what are now fairly common weather events. The study concludes that wind conditions are “safe,” yet it acknowledges wind speeds are in the official Gale force range of approximately 39 to 45 mph. These everyday conditions are near-dangerous for pedestrians, uncomfortable and disruptive for park use, and well above

thresholds known to harm birds. And all of this is occurring within a public waterfront park that also functions as a recognized ecological complex supporting bird habitat and vegetation. Save the Inlet believes that the conclusion of no significant adverse impact should be questioned by the commission and, to meet CEQR standards, a revised analysis should be required that includes pedestrian comfort criteria, full build-out of cumulative wind modeling, and multi-level wind analysis extending through the vertical range of bird flight. Given that the Bushwick Inlet is a Recognized Ecological Complex in the Waterfront Revitalization Plan, Save the Inlet wonders if the Wind Study model should include a formal ecological assessment of migratory pathways and habitat use at Bushwick Inlet, include vegetation and landscape features to reflect actual conditions, and evaluate extreme weather scenarios, including stormdriven and climate-adjusted wind patterns. Andy McDowell (ZIP code: 11222) To Whom It may Concern, While you consider granting an upzoning to the Gotham Monitor Point project, please consider the community that has been here fighting to protect our waterfront. We have been standing up - time and time and time again - to advocate for responsible development in Williamsburg and Greenpoint. I stood with neighbors over 30 years ago at the site of Marsh P Johnson State Park, when it was an abandoned lot, as we all voiced our outrage at the potential rezoning for high rises. At the time, the city and the and the property owners were framing it as a choice between waste transfer stations and oil depots or high rise apartment buildings. We were supposed to be happy that waste transfer stations would not return, despite the alternative being the essential theft of our waterfront and sky by real estate developers. Now the framing is that we need this development for "affordable" housing and to pay for Box St Park, etc. There are plenty more sites for developers to make money and also build affordable housing. Y ou do not need to sh*t on the 30 year struggle we fought to secure a smidgeon of our waterfront for park. Our fight continued along this waterfront, with small victories and big losses. Bloomberg’s rezoning plan, which ignored the neighborhood’s thorough rezoning recommendations, was a massive giveaway to moneyed real estate interests. Many of these players, with strong connections to the Bloomberg administration, bought large industrial waterfront tracts which overnight went from a value of $10M to $150M, once the Bloomberg rezoning was pushed through. Bushwick Inlet Park has come together, but at a very high cost. This is not just accounting for the staggering number of ... $500M (!!) that this park will have cost, but of the extreme community fight required to push this boulder up the hill. The battle has lasted decades, with endless advocacy invested in this very important part of our community. And now we have this waterfront green space in view, not just viable, but well underway, and behold - we are faced with the biggest of turds, ready to be laid at the very edge of our inlet, right on our park. This is an outright kick in the teeth to the entire community. Worse yet - this is proposed to happen on city owned land!!! Honestly, despite the fact that over the years while we fought for our park, groves of high rise apartment building have sprung up to steal our sky and waterfront, this particular proposal is a far more grotesque disregard for community, for this investment of effort. No amount of so-called 'affordable housing’, no landscaped waterfront pathway, no Box St Park development, and frankly no Monitor Museum promise compensates for this insult. Any of these bonuses is important in its own right, but we should not be lured into terrible deals by shiny objects. The long view is necessary. And, though we have unwisely squandered the opportunity to responsibly develop a great proportion of the Williamsburg and Greenpoint Waterfront, we can not give up now and say “Oh, what’s another high rise on the waterfront.” This entire conflict needs to be reframed. WE own that land. WE are NYC. If WE need to wait even longer for Box St Park, for the Monitor Museum, so be it. Do not give OUR sky and OUR waterfront away. Do not up zone beyond the existing as of right zoning. Leave Bushwick Inlet Park in peace! Better yet, let us aim to incorporate the Mobile Wash Facility parcel into the park! Never say never about our ability to do great things without real estate developer perks. It might take time but we can get it done.
